query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a moderate amount of chromium (Cr) into a lightweight Al-/Ti-based high-entropy alloy promotes the in situ formation of a dense composite oxide scale (Al2O3/Cr2O3) during service. This scale not only enhances corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation resistance but also refines the microstructure to improve mechanical strength while retaining low density.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight Al-/Ti-based HEA lacking significant Cr content, exhibiting a coarser microstructure and less protective native oxide film.
generation.intervention: Introduce a moderate Cr addition (on the order of 5–10 atomic %) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Performance to be evaluated under simulated aerospace and rail-transport conditions including high-temperature oxidation (around 900 °C), corrosive exposure (e.g., in 0.6 M NaCl solution), and mechanical loading regimes relevant to these applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dual-phase, adherent oxide scale (combining Al2O3 and Cr2O3) along with grain refinement in the alloy’s microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr preferentially oxidizes and combines with available Al to form a composite oxide layer that is denser and more protective than the oxide layer on the Cr-free alloy. This layer limits oxygen ingress and corrosion attack. Concurrently, Cr promotes nucleation during solidification or annealing, resulting in a refined grain structure that enhances mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline Cr-free HEA, the Cr-added alloy will exhibit lower oxidation rates (i.e., slower oxide scale growth), decreased corrosion current densities in NaCl solution, and increased yield strength due to a finer microstructure.
generation.baseline: The original lightweight Al-/Ti-based HEA without Cr addition.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to fail if the Cr content is excessively high (e.g., >15 atomic %), leading to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases rather than a beneficial oxide scale, or under conditions with insufficient oxygen partial pressure where a protective oxide layer cannot form.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in oxidation kinetics, corrosion resistance, and yield strength as well as the optimum Cr concentration remain uncertain and require systematic experimental validation across varied processing and service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: a baseline lightweight Al-/Ti-based HEA and an otherwise identical alloy with a moderate Cr addition (5–10 atomic %). Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 900 °C in air), immersion in a corrosive environment (0.6 M NaCl solution), and standardized mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests). Employ microscopic and diffraction techniques to characterize the oxide scale formation and microstructural features.
measurements: Corrosion current density and pitting potential via potentiodynamic polarization
Yield strength and ductility from mechanical tests
Grain size distribution and phase identification using SEM/TEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation and corrosion rates, fails to demonstrate microstructure refinement (or shows deleterious brittle phase formation), and does not yield improved mechanical performance compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study synthesized FeNiCuAlX high-entropy alloys (HEAs) (where X = Cr, Co, Mn) using arc melting and investigated their high-temperature oxidation behavior in air at 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of all alloys followed a parabolic rate, with the oxidation rate constants (kp) of FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn being approximately two to three orders of magnitude lower than that of the FeNiCu alloy. Specifically, FeNiCuAlCr exhibited the lowest kp value of 1.72 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s, which is significantly lower than those of FeNiCuAlCo (3.29 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s) and FeNiCuAlMn (1.71 × 10−5 mg2·cm4/s). This suggests that the addition of chromium promotes the formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer, significantly enhancing the oxidation resistance. Furthermore, corrosion resistance was assessed through potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in a 3.5% NaCl solution. FeNiCuAlCr demonstrated exceptional resistance to localized corrosion, as indicated by its low corrosion current density (45.7 μA/cm2) and high pitting potential (−0.21 V), highlighting its superior corrosion performance.

This study provides new perspectives and a new understanding of the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of high-entropy alloys, revealing their outstanding performance during the oxidation process. With the development of materials science, high-entropy alloys, as a novel material, possess great potential in industrial applications due to their superior mechanical properties, high-temperature resistance, and corrosion resistance. In the future, with continuous research, it is expected that high-entropy alloys will be widely applied in various fields such as aerospace, energy, chemical engineering, and automotive manufacturing. Especially in high-temperature, high-pressure, and extreme environments, they are expected to become important structural and functional materials.

Tseng et al. [] developed a LWHEA containing Be, with a predominant solid solution structure and low level of intermetallic phases, obtained by arc melting. The Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 (atomic percentage composition) alloy delivered unique mechanical properties and oxidation resistance which makes them appropriate for applications in the transportation industry. Sanchez et al. [] studied three lightweight high entropy alloys Al40Cu15Cr15Fe15Si15, Al65Cu5Cr5Si15Mn5Ti5 and Al60Cu10Fe10Cr5Mn5Ni5Mg5 (atomic percentage composition), which were previously designed by CALPHAD modeling. The alloys were produced by large scale vacuum die casting. Even if the cooling rate of the alloys was very low, the number of phases predicted by Thermo-Calc software was larger than those found in the experimental samples. The obtained alloys presented a high hardness to density ratio, due to the presence of complex precipitates in the as-cast structure.

reading.lever: Integrate moderate Cr addition into a lightweight Al-/Ti-based HEA to induce a protective oxide and refine microstructure.
reading.why: This composition modification, proven to enhance both oxidation and corrosion resistance in related HEA systems, directly addresses the challenge of balancing low density with multiple performance criteria.
